:::{.def}

We already saw that before images reach a model, they must be transformed into tensors with uniform size and data type, and values in a sensible range. On top of this, randomly perturbing the training images (augmentation) is a cheap way to get more out of a small dataset and prevent overtraining.

:::

## Setup

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

import torch
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, Subset
from torchvision.datasets import EuroSAT
from torchvision.transforms import v2 as T

torch.manual_seed(42)
```

[In the previous section](pt2_dataloaders.qmd#dataset-with-transform) we stored a very simple transform as an attribute of the whole dataset because we needed to convert the images to tensors to play with Dataloaders. In this section, we will create more sophisticated transforms for the validation and the training sets.

So first let's reload the dataset (without any transform this time) and [the split saved earlier](pt2_datasets.qmd#train-and-validation-sets):

```{python}
#| echo: false
root = Path("data")
```

```{.python}
root = Path("/project/def-sponsor00/data")
```

```{python}
eurosat = EuroSAT(root=root)
idx = torch.load(root/"split.pt", weights_only=True)
```

Then, let's pick a training image to work on:

```{python}
img, label = eurosat[idx["train"][0]]
print(type(img).__name__, img.size, "->", label, eurosat.classes[label])
```

## The validation pipeline

A model needs every input as a [float32]{.codelike} tensor of the same shape, with values in a comparable range. For evaluation, this conversion must be deterministic.

[`T.ToImage()`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.ToImage.html) turns the PIL image into a [uint8]{.codelike} tensor of shape `(3, 64, 64)` (channels first, which is the layout that PyTorch expects). The values are raw pixel intensities from `0` to `255`:

```{python}
x = T.ToImage()(img)
print(f"Tensor shape: {x.shape}\nTensor type: {x.dtype}\nMin, max: {int(x.min())}, {int(x.max())}")
```

[`T.ToDtype`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.ToDtype.html) with `scale=True` rescales to `[0, 1]` while converting to [float32]{.codelike} (the data type models compute in):

```{python}
x = T.ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True)(x)
print(f"Tensor shape: {x.shape}\nTensor type: {x.dtype}\nMin, max: {x.min():.3f}, {x.max():.3f}")
```

:::{.note}

Older versions of PyTorch used `transforms.ToTensor()`: the modern v2 equivalent is `ToImage()` followed by `ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True)`.

:::

[`T.Normalize`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.Normalize.html) standardizes each channel (red, green, and blue) by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. We use the mean and standard deviation of the [ImageNet dataset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ImageNet) because later in the course we will use models pretrained on ImageNet which expect inputs normalized exactly this way. We adopt them for the whole course, including our from-scratch baseline, so that every run stays comparable:

```{python}
IMAGENET_MEAN = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406]
IMAGENET_STD = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]

x = T.Normalize(IMAGENET_MEAN, IMAGENET_STD)(x)
print(f"Tensor shape: {x.shape}\nTensor type: {x.dtype}\nMin, max: {x.min():.2f}, {x.max():.2f}")
```

Let's combine the three steps together with `T.Compose`:

```{python}
val_tf = T.Compose([
    T.ToImage(),                           # PIL image -> uint8 CHW tensor
    T.ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True),  # /255 -> float32 in [0, 1]
    T.Normalize(IMAGENET_MEAN, IMAGENET_STD),
])
```

:::{.notenoit}

Our Forest patch normalizes to channel means of about −1.01, −0.65, and +0.11 (far from zero):

```{python}
print([f"{v:+.2f}" for v in x.mean(dim=(1, 2)).tolist()])
```

EuroSAT is darker and greener than the average ImageNet photo. When training a model from scratch, computing your own dataset statistics is a legitimate choice; what matters is using the same statistics everywhere for consistency.

:::

Two things are missing from this pipeline that you will usually need for your own data. EuroSAT images are all 64 × 64 pixels, so there is no [`T.Resize`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.Resize.html), and evaluation crops are deterministic, so there is no random crop. For mixed-size images, the standard evaluation recipe is `T.Resize(256)` followed by [`T.CenterCrop(224)`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.CenterCrop.html).

## The training pipeline

The number of samples of a small dataset is fixed, but the model should not keep seeing the exact same pixels. [Data augmentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_augmentation) applies random, label-preserving changes to training images at every read: the model then never trains on the same tensor twice and cannot rely on accidents of orientation or framing.

Which augmentation to chose is domain-specific: rotating handwritten digits would turn some 6s into 9s, and flipping text left to right destroys it. For satellite images which look straight down however, a field, a highway, or a lake flipped or rotated still belongs to the same class. Every augmentation you add is a bet that the change preserves the label of every image in the dataset.

Order matters: the random transforms sit before the dtype conversion because geometry on [uint8]{.codelike} tensors is cheaper than on [float32]{.codelike}, and `Normalize` must come last.

```{python}
train_tf = T.Compose([
    T.ToImage(),
    T.RandomHorizontalFlip(),  # p=0.5 by default
    T.RandomVerticalFlip(),    # p=0.5 by default
    T.RandomRotation(90),      # random angle in [-90, 90]
    T.ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True),
    T.Normalize(IMAGENET_MEAN, IMAGENET_STD),
])
```

Here is one image (a highway) next to seven passes of the random part of the pipeline:

```{python}
aug_display = T.Compose([           # for screens: without Normalize
    T.ToImage(),
    T.RandomHorizontalFlip(),
    T.RandomVerticalFlip(),
    T.RandomRotation(90),
])

img, label = eurosat[10000]
print(label, eurosat.classes[label])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(10.5, 5.5))
axes.flat[0].imshow(img)
axes.flat[0].set_title("original", fontsize=9)
axes.flat[0].axis("off")
for ax in axes.flat[1:]:
    ax.imshow(aug_display(img).permute(1, 2, 0))  # CHW -> HWC
    ax.axis("off")
```

Every call draws fresh random parameters:

```{python}
a, b, c = train_tf(img), train_tf(img), train_tf(img)
print(torch.equal(a, b), torch.equal(b, c))
```

Our 21,600 training files now yield effectively unbounded distinct training tensors: after 10 epochs, the model has seen each file 10 times, but never the same tensor twice.

And the validation transform, being deterministic, returns the identical tensor every time:

```{python}
a, b = val_tf(img), val_tf(img)
print(torch.equal(a, b))
```

[Validation and test transforms must be deterministic.]{.emph} Random transforms at evaluation time add noise to your metrics and let luck masquerade as performance. Augmentation is a training-time tool.

:::{.note}

Remember that the transforms run inside `__getitem__()`, once per sample. This means that augmentation is parallelized by the DataLoaders (based on the number of worker processes).

On this machine, one pass over the training set with 4 workers took 2.0 s without augmentation and 4.8 s with flips, rotation, and normalization. Cheap transforms keep the workers ahead of the accelerator; expensive ones [starve it again](pt2_dataloaders.qmd#data-loading-bottleneck). This means that, with augmentation, you might need to increase the number of workers to keep the GPU busy.

:::

## One draw per call

The v2 transforms also accept batches of tensors. But watch out: a transform draws one set of random parameters per call, so the whole batch gets flipped or rotated together:

```{python}
batch = torch.stack([T.ToImage()(eurosat[i][0]) for i in range(8)])
hflip = T.RandomHorizontalFlip()
for _ in range(4):
    out = hflip(batch)
    print([not torch.equal(out[i], batch[i]) for i in range(8)])
```

<br>Every line is all `True` or all `False`: never a mix. Per-sample randomness must therefore happen on the dataset side, one `__getitem__()` at a time, as we have set up.

Batched calls remain useful for deterministic transforms such as `Normalize`.

## When does augmentation help?

Augmentation is a form of regularization: it trades easy fit on the training set for generalization.

- **Training from scratch on a small dataset** (our situation in the next section): augmentation is one of the highest-value additions. The model cannot memorize exact images, and validation accuracy typically climbs once the model starts overfitting.
- **Fine-tuning a pretrained model** (a later section of this course): the backbone was already trained on millions of heavily augmented images, so it arrives robust. Start with light or no augmentation; add some back if the gap between training and validation performance grows.
- Every transform must be label-preserving **and** representative of real variation. Photometric jitter on satellite images deserves care: colour carries physical signal there (vegetation, water). Geometric flips and rotations are the safe choice for EuroSAT.

Expect the training loss to fall more slowly with augmentation: the task got harder, not the model worse. Judge on validation metrics.

For a quick strong default on natural images, torchvision also ships one-liner policies such as [`T.TrivialAugmentWide`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.TrivialAugmentWide.html) and [`T.RandAugment`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.RandAugment.html), which compose random transforms for you.

## The complete data pipeline

The data side of the course is now complete: datasets with the right transform per split, loaders with the options measured in the previous section.

```{python}
train = Subset(EuroSAT(root=root, transform=train_tf), idx["train"])
val = Subset(EuroSAT(root=root, transform=val_tf), idx["val"])
print(len(train), len(val))
```

```{python}
loader_kwargs = {
    "batch_size": 64,
    "num_workers": 4,
    "persistent_workers": True,
    "pin_memory": torch.accelerator.is_available(),
}
train_loader = DataLoader(train, shuffle=True, **loader_kwargs)
val_loader = DataLoader(val, **loader_kwargs)
```

One training batch:

```{python}
x, y = next(iter(train_loader))
print(x.shape, x.dtype, f"{x.min():.2f} {x.max():.2f}")
print(y[:8].tolist())
```

Augmented, normalized, shuffled batches of tensors now flow at steady state. What is still missing is the model and the loop that trains it: this is the next section.
